title: Elizabeth Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Elizabeth wells have a 355-foot median depth, 12 gpm median yield, and typical completed costs of $23,800-$36,800.
h1: What Elizabeth, Colorado Wells Cost and Produce
intro_html:
Buying land around Elizabeth means looking closely at the well record before you rely on a driller’s estimate. The records within 5 miles show a Denver Basin setting, with wells commonly completed in the Upper Dawson, unnamed fractured-bedrock, or Lower Dawson aquifers. Among wells reporting the relevant measurements, the median depth is 355 feet and the median reported pump yield is 12.0 gallons per minute.

That is useful local guidance, not a guarantee for a specific parcel. Ground conditions can change across short distances, and the permit file may not include every detail you need. Check nearby wells, confirm the intended use, and have a Colorado well professional review the permit and construction records before closing.

sections.heading: Elizabeth well depth: plan for the Denver Basin
sections.html:
Elizabeth-area wells are usually deeper than a shallow domestic well. The median completed depth is 355 feet, with the middle half between 295 and 435 feet. About 61% of wells fall between 300 and 600 feet, while 13% are deeper than 600 feet. The deepest recorded well reaches 2,318 feet, showing how widely local conditions can vary.

For a drilling bid, the 295-to-435-foot range is more useful than the median alone. A lot with nearby wells around the upper end of that range may need a larger drilling allowance than a lot surrounded by shallower records. Permits name the Upper Dawson most often, followed by unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifers and the Lower Dawson. All named permit aquifers are within the Denver Basin system.

sections.heading: Expected well yield near Ponderosa Park and Franktown
sections.html:
The median reported pump yield near Elizabeth is 12.0 gallons per minute, and the middle half runs from 10.0 to 14.5 gallons per minute. Most reported wells, 74%, produce between 5 and 15 gallons per minute. Another 25% report more than 15 gallons per minute, while 1% report between 1 and 5 gallons per minute. No reported wells in this set are under 1 gallon per minute.

Those figures suggest a generally workable range for household planning, but a yield test is still important. Pump yield is not the same as storage in the well or a guarantee during drought. Review the well permit’s allowed use and household restrictions. An exempt household-use well also has a 35-gpm pumping limit, even if a particular well can produce more.

sections.heading: Elizabeth water levels: variable, not a straight decline
sections.html:
Reported static water levels have a median depth of 180 feet below the surface, with the middle half between 125 and 240 feet. That affects pump sizing, electrical planning, and the cost of bringing water into a house. A water level is a snapshot taken at a particular time, so it should not be treated as the same thing as the well’s total depth.

The decade medians move around rather than showing a steady one-way trend: 135 feet in the 1970s, 164 in the 1980s, 230 in the 1990s, 204 in the 2000s, 170 in the 2010s, and 205 in the 2020s. The record does not support claiming a simple continuing drop. Because only 236 wells report a static water level, ask for the actual neighboring measurements and recent pump information for the parcel you are considering.

sections.heading: Who drilled Elizabeth wells, and when permits were active
sections.html:
Elizabeth’s permit history reflects sustained rural and residential development. The records contain 5,334 permitted wells, with 3,612 recorded as constructed. Permit activity was highest in the 1990s, when 1,495 permits were issued. The 1980s had 909, the 1970s had 805, the 2000s had 732, the 2010s had 441, and the 2020s had 275. The newest permit year in the records is 2025.

The most common drillers in these records are Hamacher Well Works Inc, also listed with Alan Ray Hamacher, at 1,088 wells; Hier Drilling Co Inc, with Bruce A. Hier, at 635; and Parker Drilling/Pump Service Inc., with Tommy E. Thrasher, at 577. Those names help identify local permit history, but they are not a recommendation or a substitute for current references and a written scope of work.

sections.heading: Elizabeth well drilling cost at typical local depths
sections.html:
The cost model for Elizabeth assumes Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock and a drilling rate of $50 to $70 per foot. At the 355-foot median depth, the drilled hole alone is estimated at about $17,800 to $24,800. A finished system, including the pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical work, is estimated at about $23,800 to $36,800.

Use those figures as a budgeting range, not a fixed quote. Depth is the biggest visible driver, but access, casing and grout requirements, pump setting, trench length, electrical service, and site conditions can change the final number. Ask each bidder what is included and what happens if the hole must be deepened. A low drilling price that excludes the pump, tank, trenching, or electrical work is not comparable to a completed-well estimate.

sections.heading: Risks to check before buying an Elizabeth lot
sections.html:
Low yield is not the main signal in this record, but dry holes and disappointing production can still occur because Denver Basin and fractured-bedrock conditions vary by location. Confirm neighboring well depths, yields, static levels, and construction details rather than relying only on countywide summaries. The well’s permitted use also matters: 92% of the use records include domestic or household use, while some include stock or irrigation.

Water quality deserves its own review. Mapped environmental information within about 10 miles includes 20 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 1 historic mine feature, and 2 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. That does not prove a problem at a particular home. Test the existing well, identify nearby environmental sites, and keep septic setbacks and the proposed building location in the site plan. A new septic system and a new well need coordinated placement and access.

sections.heading: A practical plan for building near Elizabeth
sections.html:
Before you buy, pull the Colorado DWR permit and construction records for the parcel and compare them with nearby wells in Elizabeth, Ponderosa Park, Franktown, and Kiowa. Look for a cluster of depths near the 295-to-435-foot middle range, but budget for the possibility that your site differs. Ask for a current water-quality test and a documented production test where an existing well is present.

For vacant land, obtain a written drilling proposal that separates the hole from the finished system. Confirm the intended household, stock, or irrigation use and check whether an augmentation plan is required in the applicable over-appropriated basin. Before construction, coordinate well access, septic placement, electrical routing, driveway work, and the house site. The records provide a strong local starting point; parcel-specific review is what turns it into a buying decision.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Elizabeth, Colorado?
faq.a: The median well depth within 5 miles of Elizabeth is 355 feet. The middle half runs from 295 to 435 feet, and 61% of reported depths fall between 300 and 600 feet. Some wells are much deeper, with the deepest record at 2,318 feet, so nearby permits are more useful than the median alone when estimating a new well.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Elizabeth, Colorado?
faq.a: At the local modeled rate of $50 to $70 per foot, a 355-foot hole is estimated at $17,800 to $24,800. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical work is estimated at $23,800 to $36,800. Actual bids can change with depth, access, casing and grout, pump requirements, trench length, and electrical conditions.

faq.q: How much water do Elizabeth wells produce?
faq.a: The median reported pump yield near Elizabeth is 12.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half between 10.0 and 14.5 gallons per minute. About 74% of reported wells produce between 5 and 15 gallons per minute. These are area records, not a guarantee for a new hole, so request a yield test and review the neighboring wells.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Elizabeth, Colorado?
faq.a: The permit records do not establish that every well is safe to drink. Environmental mapping within about 10 miles includes 20 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 1 historic mine feature, and 2 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Test the specific well for relevant contaminants, review nearby site information, and retest if the property, water quality, or land use changes.

faq.q: Should I check a well before buying land near Elizabeth?
faq.a: Yes. Review the Colorado DWR permit, construction record, permitted use, depth, yield, and static water level. The local median depth is 355 feet, the median yield is 12.0 gallons per minute, and the median static water level is 180 feet below the surface. Compare those figures with nearby wells and arrange water testing before relying on the property’s supply.
